Aufgabe 3 was done by two learners.  Both of them struggled a bit with the fact that they had to write opposing essays,
one emphasizing that it is a good thing to buy, buy, buy and the other essay focusing on “less is more”.  Both learners
were more successful in one of the parts of the topic.  Both learners only touched on the buying habits of teenagers.  The
last fact being mentioned in the topic itself.  Paragraphs were generally well observed.  Here as well, one learner spent
quite  some  time  on Aufgabe  1  and  thus  must  have  run  out  of  time  for Aufgabe  3,  as  that  learner  did  not  write  enough
words, which influenced the content mark awarded.  The introduction and the first paragraph were well written, for the
marker to be looking forward to “the rest of the essay”.
This examination session the form proved no difficulty to the learners, as well as the time frame of two hours, for twice
600    to    900    words    altogether    for  Aufgabe    1    and    then    one  Aufgabe    of   Teil    B.        Generally,    learners    seemed    to    be    well
prepared for the time frame, although two learners really struggled with using their time wisely.  The use of vocabulary,
more complex sentences and the structuring of the arguments were presented on different levels.  Learners have to be
encouraged to cover all aspects of the topic, although the new syllabus allows for a wide range of arguments. Learners
should    also    be    guided    in    providing    depth    for    their    arguments.        It    was    pleasing    to    see    that    all    five    learners    did    their
planning.

For    the    first    language    learners,    teachers    could    revise    the    use    of    the    letter    “v”    and    when    to    use    “f”,    e.g.,    Fortschritt,

The subject German First Language was written during the second week of the examination session.  Languages are
practical subjects and with all the other subjects being written in English, the later learners write German the greater
are    the    chances    of    them    demonstrating    “weaker”    language    skills.        Writing    the    paper    in    the    second    week    was    much

GENERAL COMMENTS
This was the third written external examination under the new syllabus.  Five candidates have written this paper.

In this paper candidates are presented with 12 (twelve) questions.  The examination paper consists of three sections.
Section 1 offers an A and a B question with regard to the prescribed poems. Section 2 offers six questions, two questions
(A and B) covering the prescribed short stories, two questions (A and B) covering “Die verlorene Ehre der Katharina
Blum”  and  two  questions  (A  and  B)  covering  “Homo  Faber”.    Section  3  offers  the  candidates  four  questions.   The  first
two (A and B) cover the drama “Der gute Mensch von Sezuan” and the other two (A and B) cover the drama “Die
Physiker”. Altogether candidates have to answer two questions, coming from two different sections.  Each answer has
to be between 600 and 900 words in length, although the question paper does not mention it specifically to allow for a
creative approach.  The A questions in each section are without any text extract, whereas all the B questions have an
extract of the prose, drama, short stories or poem.  The candidates coped with the length of the answers, it was obvious
that the B sections were mastered better and one candidate opted for the A section, but struggled to include quotations.
Paragraphs were observed, and introduction as well as a conclusive paragraph to end the essay properly.
Two candidates chose to answer question B of the poems, and were successful in aligning their interpretational essay
in sequence of the poem, while including their personal response in the concluding paragraph.  Three candidates
chose B question of the short stories, where they had to relate to the boy in the class room and his view to life.  Having
concentrated     more     on     this     first     essay,     most     candidates     could     obtain     better     marks     than     for     the     second     essay.         This
shows, that the time factor plays a major role, where candidates are measured on a first language standard, while their
language of instruction for all other subjects is in English and thus it does not benefit them to have a general background
knowledge of German suitable to be at ease with their process of thinking and writing.

For the second question to be answered from a different section, all candidates opted for the drama “Die Physiker”. The
weakest candidate opted for section A and sidelined the instruction of “Die Rolle Salomos”, while concentrating more on
the general content of the Drama and the interaction of its different role players.
The B section required the analysis of the Characters with their attitude to “Freiheit auf sozialer, politischer und
wissenschaftlicher Ebene”.  Where the candidates analysed all three aspects, they could master substantial arguments
to      benefit      their      content      mark.            One      candidate      concentrated      mainly      on      retelling      the      story      with      hardly      analyzing      the
contents.

In general, it can be said that although all candidates were well prepared for the questions they chose, some struggled
to adjust to the specific question and the ending with some of the second essays were rather abrupt to fit into the given
time.  All of them had their own approach to analyze the texts, short stories or poems, which show that the method of
teaching used were open and allowed for personal responses to the literature.
The subject German First Language was written early in the examination session.  Languages are practical subjects
and with all the other subjects being written in English, the later learners write German the greater are the chances of
them demonstrating “weaker” language skills.  Writing the paper early in the exam session was much appreciated and
the open individual approaches were lively and refreshing to mark.

GENERAL COMMENTS

There is a decline in the performance of the candidates during this examination compared to the 2022 examination.

Some candidates understood the language used by the authors and the effectiveness of the indicative language given
in the reading texts.  Well done on that.

However, there were a few candidates that did not understood the effect the author was creating based on the language
used in the text.

Teachers are advised to encourage learners to engage in consistent practice of spelling and language usage to enhance
their writing abilities, as these imperfections can occasionally impede the comprehension of candidates’ work.

Some candidates found the b questions, such as 1(b) or 2(b), to be exceptionally difficult.  The candidates were required
to recreate a piece of writing that closely resembled the original texts using the information provided in the passage.
Without considering what was being asked, the majority of candidates copied the passage verbatim into their responses.

The candidate continues to respond to Part A in the form of a poem, utilising stars or bullet points, or in extremely brief
sentences, without providing any analysis, despite the matter having been addressed in the 2022 examiner ’s report.

Some candidates still named the punctuation marks used by the author in answering of question A’s, although there
was no relevance in what the author aimed to bring fourth with these punctuation marks and how it contributes to the
style of the writing piece.

There is a distinct difference between figures of speech and figurative language used by the authors, please teach the
candidate to differentiate between the two and always show appreciation to the style of the author by explaining why it
is used in certain instances e.g. “Afrikab !khō-omdi” this title may be used with inverted commas by the author to show
the readers that we have enslaved ourselves and our continent with our mind-set.

A  few  candidates  were  unable  to  finish  the  question  (b’s),  and  a  lot  of  blank  spaces  were  observed  as  they  aimed  to
first  answer  the  (a)  questions  before  the  (b)  questions.    Some  candidates  failed  to  answer  all  questions  because  they
wasted time rewriting questions.

Candidates do not consider the marks allocated to the questions, especially in the (a) questions, where some of the
candidates’ work was very short and showed very little appreciation of the author ’s work.

Some of  the candidates used a range of rhetorical devices to explain, argue, or persuade in discursive or argumentative
writing,   and   their   use   of   figurative   language   in   descriptive   or   narrative   writing   produced   particular   linguistic   effects   on
the marker or reader.

The candidates could express themselves freely by using a wide range of language effects effectively.

Some candidates were unable to attain high grades on this paper due to what appears to be a lack of guidance from
their teachers regarding the critical analysis of authors’ styles and language usage (e.g., “xoa-aob ge tsotsi midiʁuiba ra
sisenū”).  Which styles is the candidate referring to?  The aforementioned candidates achieved commendable marks on
the directed writing assessment.  Low academic performance was noted at some centres as a consequence.

COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS


1     This question is compulsory.  This was a speech written by Leymah R. Gbowee, polemic/argumentative/
      dogmatic and has a mixture of formal and informal language on the state of the African continent                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                .  It
      consists of two parts:

      (a)   The candidates were required to comment on the style and language of the author to convey the
            strength of her opinion about the state of the African continent.
            The majority of the candidates demonstrated that they had received proper guidance on identifying
            various styles used by the author and understood that the author ’s style consisted of convincing the audience
            to accept her theory that Africa is mismanaged by those entrusted with its leadership and that only bad things
            occur  there.    Certain  candidates  have  even  contended  that  the  author ’s  writing  styles  are  in  conflict  with  her
            intentions, given that the speech’s title is enclosed inverted commas and is emphasised multiple times.  This
            implies that while the notion of a new Africa does not reflect reality, it is possible for an innovation to emerge
            from it.

            Despite this, a subset of candidates merely comprehend and list the figurative material present in the assigned
            readings without providing an explanation of its authorial purpose or its contribution to the overall message.
            Some candidates submitted their part A responses in the form of poems or bullet points, using brief sentences
            that do not align with the criteria outlined in the marking grid used to award marks for this task.

            It was evident that some centres did not teach candidates on how this question should be answered.   Candidates
            only attempted to mention the style of the author and re-wrote the whole passage without recognition of
            authors style or language and how it has contributed to the question at hand.  Candidate could not achieve
            good marks due to this and low marks were observed at some centres.

      (b)   A directed writing task to write a response to the speech written by Leymah R. Gbowee titled
            “20 years of progress in Africa”.
            Candidates were expected to write the opposing speech to the views of the original texts.  Some candidates
            once again did not clearly understand the instructions and wrote the same destructions mentioned by the
            original texts and how Africans will continue to cross the sea and that corruption will not be stopped.
            There were a few candidates that wrote the opposing speech very well and mentioned how Africans can
            change as Madiba was also freed from prison and was a better version of himself.  Motivating Africans to raise
            up and do better and to free themselves from their minds.  Recognising Africa’s resources and how it can be
            beneficial to everyone with visionary leaders.

2     This was the most popular question adapted from the Biography of Barrack Obama.  It consists of two parts:

      (a)   The candidates were required to comment on the style and language of the author to convey the
            strength of Obama’s sense of feeling at home in Kenya.
            This question was well answered, as most of the candidates could link and understand the style of the author
            by explaining the reasons for the use of certain words and phrases to show the good feeling Obama had
            before he arrived in Kenya and how suddenly circumstances changed in Kenya and how lonely and unloved
            he felt when he was not welcomed at the airport.  Some candidates however were unable to see the difference
            in the destinations that Obama visited and Kenya, thus candidates mentioned his feelings in Hawaii when he
            was with his mother and stepmother and not when he was in Kenya.

      (b)   This was a directed writing task to write a letter, as Auma, Obama’s half-sister to a relative about
            meeting young Obama in Kenya.
            Most candidates understood and did exceptionally well in this question; the letter clearly explained the
            excitement that was felt when young Obama was met at the airport and how uncertain he seemed to meet his
            people after so many years.  Some candidates even added characters similar to Obama’s that they claimed
            made them think about his father and that he resembles him in every way.

            However:
            Some candidates misunderstood the instructions and wrote a letter as the grandmother of Obama and was
            asking how he was welcomed at the airport or copied his experiences from the original texts.  Auma was his
            half-sister that welcomed him at the airport and not his grandmother, the instruction clearly stated that the
            candidates should write about the time they meet in Kenya.  But some candidates wrote about his time in
            Hawaii or his other trips with the friends.  Once again, misinterpretation of questions causes candidates to
            score low marks.  They should be encouraged to understand what is expected from a question before they
            attempt to answer the questions by identifying key words.

3     This story was adapted from the book, “The Pearl” and was a narrative piece of writing:  This part had two
      questions as well.  The question was the least answered question in this paper.

      (a)   The candidates were required to comment on the style and language of the author to convey how the
            people in the town reacted to Kino’s finding the Pearl.
            Most of the candidates could understand how the author used the different characters in this texts to portray
            the importance of the pearl in this town and could effectively analysis the indicative content or language used.
            Some candidates were unable to connect the author ’s aims of characterisation of the characters and the effect
            thereof on Kino’s past.  Some candidates copied the reading texts as it appears word by word, which is not
            expected from candidates at this level.

      (b)   A directed writing task to write a diary entry as if they were Kino.
            Most candidates wrote a touchy yet realistic diary entry of Kino, mentioning his struggles in the morning before
            he got the pearl.  The excitement yet uncertainty of the pearl and its value is clearly brought up in the writing.

            Some candidates wrote their diary entry of different dates, however if instructions are understood correctly
            he must write a diary entry of that day when he found the pearl.  Candidates should read the questions to
            comprehend what they are expected to write before answering the question.

•     We are aware of the different challenges we are faced with as teachers and you are applauded for your efforts,
      however please don’t stop to re-enforce on your teachings daily.

•     We should teach our candidates how to answer the different questions in this question paper and to enable them
      to recognise and analyse different languages effects used in different texts.  This will boost Khoekhoegowab First
      Language performance.

•     The       Senior       Education       Officers       and       Head       of       Departments       should       ensure       that       the       teachers       receive       a       copy       of
      this document.  Diligent efforts are encouraged to train teachers on effectively on the implementation of the
      recommendations mentioned in this report.

•     Teach learners to read and understand questions as in most cases candidates appeared to have read part of the
      question and start answering thus resulting in them losing marks.

•     Train learners how to identify keywords in different types of questions.  Candidates should ensure that if hint are
      given in questions, they should restrict their answers to those details that support the hint instead of dwelling on
      general responses on language and style.

•     The marking grid should be used to train the learners on the expected standard and on how Questions (a)s and (b)
      s should be answered.

•     Candidates should be exposed to a variety of reading materials so that they can be able respond to longer piece
      questions and make their writing interesting and full of vocabulary.

•     In conjunction with the syllabus and the Khoekhoegowab 3rd Edition orthography should be used to avoid
      unnecessary grammatical errors.

•     Teachers should caution learners to use figures of speech correctly and in collaboration with the authors intention
      and not in vain.

•     Centres and teachers are applauded for their hard work amidst strenuous circumstances and limited resources.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Performance:      This was the third examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Oshikwanyama.  The
performance      of      candidates      was      notably      moderate      compared      with      the      first      and      second      examinations.          A      significant
number of centres could satisfactorily meet the expectations of the syllabus.  There is recognizable evidence that after
three years of teaching Oshikwanyama First Language at this level, the quality of teaching and learning is improving.
It was an immense pleasure to observe the good language skills and grammar usage exhibited by the candidates from
some centres.  Some candidates displayed a better use of figurative language through their sensitive and discriminating
awareness of language and style.  Those centres and teachers who consistently put more effort into their teaching and
learning are noted and applauded!

Time constraint:  It was observed that a number of candidates were caught up in time and could not complete.  This
could be attributed to them writing unnecessarily long responses to the (a) questions, which have no word restriction.
It was also observed that some candidates wrote long responses for Question 1(b), 2(b) and 3(b) which have word
restrictions (120–150 words)                                                                                                                                                                                        .

Passages:   It appeared that the three passages (persuasive, narrative, and descriptive) on which the questions were
based were fairly understood by the majority of the candidates who sat for the examination.  Of the two elective
questions, Question 2 appeared to be the most popular, although a good number of candidates also attempted Question
3.  Candidates who attempted to answer Question 3 performed better than those who opted to answer Question 2.
However, most candidates performed worse in Question 2 than in Questions 1 and 3.

GENERAL COMMENTS
Performance:  This was the third examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Oshindonga.  The performance
of candidates was notably moderate compared with the first and second examinations.  A significant number of centres
could satisfactorily meet the expectations of the syllabus.  There is a recognisable evidence that after three years of
teaching Oshindonga First Language at this level, the quality of teaching and learning is increasing well.  It was an
immense pleasure to observe the good language skills and grammar usage exhibited by the candidates from some
centres.  Some candidates displayed a better good use of figurative language through their sensitive and discriminating
awareness of language and style.  Those centres and teachers who consistently put more effort in their teaching and
learning are noted and applauded!

Time constraint:  It was observed that a number of candidates were caught up in time and could not complete.  This
could be attributed to them writing unnecessarily long responses to the (a) questions which has no word restriction.
It was also observed that some candidates wrote long responses for Question 1 (b), Question 2 (b)  and Question 3 (b)
which have words restriction (120 – 150 words).

Passages:  It appeared that the three passages (persuasive, narrative and descriptive) on which the questions
were set, were fairly understood by the majority of the candidates who set for the examination.  Of the two elective
questions, Question 2 appeared to be the most popular, although a good number of candidates also attempted Question
3. Candidates who attempted to answer question 3 performed better than those who opted to answer Question 2.
However, most candidates performed poorer in Question 2 than in Question 1 and 3.

COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

Question 1
The questions were based on a speech by Leymah R. Gbowee on the theme:  “The prisons of Africa”.  The passage is
a speech to African leaders on the power of compassion to humanize and unite people and to a mobilizing for change
as demonstrated by Mandela.

This question consists of two parts, parts (a) and (b).  Part (a) requires the candidates to comment on how the author
uses language and style to convey his point of view, while part (b) is a directed writing task that requires the candidates
to write one part of an article based on the writer ’s original speech.

           about the state of the African continent.  In response to this question, candidates had to display, through good
           use of language and style similar to that of the passage, their knowledge and understanding of the passage as
           well as the authors’ intentions.  This was a persuasive passage that was written in a formal, persuasive, and
           relaxed mood.  The author uses a variety of strong, and persuasive vocabulary.
           Candidates   who   performed   better,   were   the   ones   who   figured   out   that   the   author ’s   aim   of   the   passage   was
           to persuade African leaders on the power of compassion to humanize and unite people and to mobilize for
           change.

           Candidates must be able to identify words and phrases that persuade and reassure readers throughout the
           passage and link them to quotations that underline the author's point of view in order to give a strong response
           to this question.

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS

•	   Learners	need	to	read	and	understand	the	whole	question	before	attempting	it,	because	in	most	cases	candidates
     only	read	part	of	the	questions	and	start	answering	it,	thus	resulting	in	them	losing	marks.

•	   Learners	need	exposure	to	different	places	where	they	will	have	opportunities	to	see	unique	places	such	as	the
     Sea,	the	Desert	etc.,	so	that	they	could	always	relate	whenever	they	are	writing	essays.

•	   Learners	need	to	be	taught	on	how	to	identify	keywords	in	different	types	of	questions.

•	   The	marking	grid	should	be	used	to	teach	learners	on	the	expected	standard	and	how	section	(Section	A	imaginative
     writing	and	Section	B	writing	for	an	Audience)	should	be	answered.

•	   Learners	should	to	be	exposed	to	a	diverse	range	of	reading	materials	in	order	to	develop	the	capacity	to	respond
     to	lengthier	piece	questions.	This	will	enable	them	to	produce	writing	that	is	both	engaging	and	characterised	by	an
     extensive	vocabulary.
•	   In	order	for	candidates	to	gain	experience	writing	two	contrasting	pieces	in	the	same	question,	practical	questioning
     must	take	place	at	centres.

•	   In	conjunction	with	the	syllabus	outline	and	other	pertinent	Oshindonga	First	Language	resources,	the	most	recent
     edition	of	the	Oshindonga	First	Language	orthography	should	be	used	to	prevent	unnecessary	grammatical	errors.

•	   Teachers	should	teach	learners	on	different	types	of	tasks,	that	are	likely	to	be	asked	in	Section	A	and	Section	B,
     respectively.

•	   Teachers	should	teach	learners	on	how	to	use	the	punctuation	marks.

Centers	and	teachers	are	applauded	for	their	hard	work	amidst	strenuous	circumstances	and	limited	resources.

Thank	you	for	all	your	efforts!

1.    GENERAL COMMENTS
      Performance:  This one was the third examination to be taken as NSSCAS First Language Otjiherero.  The
      performance of candidates was notably poorer when compared with the first and second examinations.  A significant
      number of centres could not satisfactorily meet the expectations of the syllabus.  There is regrettable evidence that
      after three years of teaching Otjiherero at this level, the quality of teaching and learning is dropping.  It could be
      clearly deduced from the candidates’ responses that at a number of centres the quality of teaching is very poor and
      worse no teaching and learning is taking place at some centres!  Those centres and teachers who consistently put
      more effort in their teaching and learning are noted and applauded!

      Time constraint:  It was observed that a number of candidates were caught up in time and could not complete.
      This could be attributed to them writing unnecessarily long responses to the first question especially Question 1 (b)
      which has a word restriction (120 – 150 words).

      Passages:      It   appeared   that   the   three   passages   (persuasive,   narrative   and   descriptive)   on   which   the   questions
      were set, were fairly understood by the majority of the candidates who sat for the examination.  Of the two elective
      questions,     Question     3     appeared     to     be     slightly     the     most     popular     (with     77     out     of     the     140     candidates     attempting
      it)    although    a    good    number    of    candidates    (63    out    of    the    140)    also    attempted    Question    2.       The    performance    of
      candidates on Questions 2 and 3 were almost the same.  However, most candidates performed poorer in Question
      1 than in Question 2 or 3.

      Excerpts from weak and strong answers:  As with previous reports, excerpts from strong and weak answers
      are given to assist teachers in their preparation.  Candidates should not be led to memorise wordings from strong
      answers with a view of reproducing them indiscriminately when given different passages and questions.

     only	read	part	of	the	question	and	start	answering	thus	resulting	in	them	losing	marks.

     the	Sea,	the	Desert	etc.,	so	that	they	could	always	relate	whenever	they	are	writing	essays.

•	   Candidates	need	to	be	trained	on	how	to	identify	keywords	in	different	types	of	questions.

•	   The	marking	grid	should	be	used	to	train	the	candidates	on	the	expected	standard	and	on	how	section	(Section	A
     imaginative	writing	and	Section	B	writing	for	an	Audience)	should	be	answered.

1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

Overall, the question paper seems to be easier than the 2022 Examination paper because for each question, there
were learners who answered;  compared to last year where most of the learners concentrated only on a few questions.

To add on, some candidates did not pay attention to the keywords in each question before answering.

There are also candidates who have problems on orthography, punctuation, spelling and vocabulary.  In addition to that,
some sentences did not make sense at all, as some wrote words with very small letters that were too small to see.  In
some instances, the letters were big but they were not clear to the reader.  On the other hand, there were candidates
who did marvelously as their essays had good spelling, vocabulary, orthography, usage of proverbs/idioms and well
constructed paragraphs.

3.     POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
•      Teachers deserve praise for their endeavour and excellent effort in preparing candidates for examinations.
•      Teachers are encouraged to use previous question papers and specimens to train learners on interpretation of the
       main topics and subtopics of the question.
•      Teachers are encouraged to read examiners’ reports and share them with the learners.
•      Teachers are encouraged to teach orthographic writing.
•      Candidates need to be exposed to different writing in the media such as newspaper correspondence, speeches
       and voiceover scripts to learn tone, as well as register the format of each writing.
•      Teachers are encouraged to help candidates on how to create and construct ideas.
•      Teachers need to expose candidates to a wide range of vocabulary and the translation of certain words to avoid
       English usage and spelling errors.
•      Candidates need to be provided a marking scheme so they understand it and know what is expected of them in a
       good essay.  They must take note of 1. Mutungo 2. Edemeneno 3. Ndunganesoraka 4.Yidivisoreseso
•      Teachers should encourage candidates to stick to prescribed word length of 500 to 600 words in each section.
•      Vamitili va ronge nonsingononinkangodina.
•      Vamitili va ronge yiruwo eyi aga simbi mapuro.
•      Teachers are urged to instruct candidates on various types of letter, format and information.
•      When teaching language usage, emphasis should be focus on punctuation, spelling, sentence building, idioms and
       phrases.  Eyi mulyo unene komutungontanto ntani sisewe si li ze neyi ono kutjanga.
•      Teachers are urged to instruct candidates on how to write creatively and for an audience.
•      Candidates should be encouraged to use linking words.
•      Teachers should encourage learners to write clearly and neatly.

1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

The overall performance of the candidates was not good in this Examination Paper 1.  It was observed that candidates
struggled to answer the questions as their work lacked the quality expected.  However, there were a few candidates who
tried to answer some questions well.  In most cases candidates only answered question (a) and left question (b) or they
made a slight attempt at writing a few sentences.

Candidates did not do well in Question 1 (a), (b) and because of the fact that it is a compulsory question, it dragged
down the candidate’s performance.  Most of them misinterpreted this question due to some words and proverbs that
were    used    in    the    text.       They    misunderstood    the    content    of    the    text.        Furthermore,    question    2    text    contained    difficult
language above the candidates’ level.  Even though a high number of candidates chose this question, they could not
put in more effort or show some skills to meet the demand of being able to provide clear understanding and to analyze
the author ’s idea, as well as be able to identify the language and style which require knowledge and understanding.
Question 3 was chosen by a few candidates and those who did so, could not do well in all the parts of the question.

In Question 1, 2, 3 (a) candidates were required to comment on the language and style and in that way, they should
identify the language and style which require knowledge and understanding, as well as analysis of language effects

“Go ne go kokotiwa kwa godimo fa kgorong.  Erile ke bula, ka bona mosimanyana a gatsetse mo letsididing la phakela.”
Kwala ka ga maikutlo le ditiro tsa moaned:  Mo tlhamong ya gago kwala ka letshogo le bosaitsiweng.

Moithuti ga a kwala jalo jalo ka maikutlo, letshogo le bosaitsiweng.  Moithuti o kwadile fela gore o bone mosimanyana
a kokotha a gatsetse mme a tlelwa ke letshogo jang, ga a kwala, ka bonako fela a mo utlwela botlhoko.  Ditema tsa
moithuti di ne di sena kgogedi epe mo motlhatlhobing, go sena le manatetshapuo kgotsa diane.  Moithuti o ne a
tshwanetse a kwale a lebisitse mo maikutlong a gagwe sekai:

Erile fa ke utlwa mokokotho o kwa godimo o sa tlwaelegang ka tsenwa ke letshogo la gore e ka bo go rileng fa o kare
motho yo o kokothang o tla a lelekisiwa ke sengwe se se tshosang.

Fa ke bula kgoro ke se ka ka dumela matlho ame, go ka bona mosimanyana a le mo seemong se se utlwisang botlhoko
jana ka maphakela mo serameng se se botlhoko jana.  Ka ema sebakanyana fa kgorong o kare ke a lora, mme e se go
lora mogopolo wa me o tlhamuketse ka dipotso tse dintsi tse di. senang dikarabo.  Ka kua rraabo go tswa ko phaposing
ya borobalo go tla go ntshebisa se ke se bonang.  Mo go fitlheng ga gagwe le ene a tla asa rwala le ditlhako a tshogile
go utlwa ke mo kua ka mokgwa o sa tlwaelegang.  Ka sedikwa ke ntsa pedi se se thata, erile go goroga fa kgorong a re.

“Ao mosimanyana wa batho maemo a bosa a e a sa iketla maabane mo go raya gore erile basa ntse ba le kwa nageng
ba disitse dipudi diphefo tse di maatla tsa ba tshwara tsa ba timetsa go boela kwa gae.  Tsa mo ralatsa naga go fitlhela
lefifi  le  lentsho  le  tsena.   A  ipolelela  gore  mo  nageng  ga  ke  robale  ke  tshwanetse  ka  tsamaya  fela  go  fitlhela  ke  bona
lesedinyana gongwe.

Ke ka moo a bo neng lesedinyana la magala a molelo wa maabane fa ga rona, a ipolelela gore o a sala morago ao
matlhotlhapelo ruri”.

Mosimanyana o ne a lebega a letse bosigo jotlhe mo serameng fa o lebelela seemo sa gagwe, le moaparo o ne a apere
letsatsanyana fela.  O bona jaaka a tshedile fela ka letshoba la nnale, o ne a saletswe fela ke go wela fatshe a jewa ke
diphologolo tsa naga, o bona le gore tlala e mo tshwere ga go sepe mo maleng.

Mosadi wa batho a tsenwa ke mahutsana a ipotsa dipotso gore fa e kabo e le ngwanake a e tshwara ka fa bogaleng
mosadi wa batho a tlola a gotsa molelo fa rrabo a ntse a mo apola diaparo tse di wetsweng ke serame a mo apesa tsa
setlogolo sa gagwe.  Mosadi a mo direla mogodungwane ba mo nosa ka ane a palelwa ke go itshwarela sejana. Ka
ebile le puo e ne e pala go tswa ka molomo, ke bona jaaka ngwana wa batho a tla go ragela thokolo mo game ke sala
ke araba dilo tse ke sa di itsing.

1.   GENERAL COMMENTS

Most candidates answered question 1 and 2.  Most of those who understood the passages, expressed themselves fairly
well.  There was an evident level of clear detail and accurate understanding in 2a- and 3a-compared to 1 a-b, 2b and 3b.

There were relatively few cases of response on question area which was not answered completely.  When these
occurred, it was most often towards the last question.  Perhaps time was short, although it may also have been because
of excessive writing on (a) questions (2-3 full pages) which is mostly unnecessary.

Candidates  successfully  identified  language  features  but  were  not  so  good  at  commenting  on  the  language  and  style
in Thimbukushu (a) questions.  To repeat, focus on language commentary.  One way to do so, is to say if the author is
being successful in the message being communicated and what is implied and inferred with reference to the language
from the passage to support the inference.  There was also a tendency to write too many words in all questions.  It is
acceptable in the (a) questions but not up to 3 pages full with repeated language mistakes.

Copying (‘lifting’) of material to answer the entire question was one of the reasons for marks not being awarded in (b)
questions.  However, most candidates also did not draw a line of the b questions.  Some also wrote too many words
on (b) questions especially a whole page or page and a half for 120 – 150 words?  This was mostly done by those who
instead of rewording the language copied and over-copied.  Some became over creative and reworded the same ideas.

2.    COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC QUESTIONS


The speaking examination for the AS German Foreign Language consists of three parts.


Every     year     there     are     five     general     topics     available     for     the   AS     German     Foreign     Language     candidates     and     they     then
choose   one   of   the   topics   to   do   their   presentation   on,   going   into   more   detail   on   that   specific   topic.      Thus,   there   is   no
question paper available, only a mark scheme for this specific examination.  This year all five general topics were spoken
about,  the  most  popular  one  being  education,  health  and  fitness,  while  the  least  used  ones  were  nature  conservation
and technological innovations.


Part A being a presentation by each candidate which should not be longer than three minutes.  Overall, this was not a
problem, although some candidates were allowed to present for almost four minutes.  It should be mentioned that three
minutes  are  sufficient  and  that  candidates  may  be  stopped.   The  rest  of  the  presentation  (should  there  be  some  part)
could be used for the second part, where questions are asked about the presentation of the candidate.  One centre had
misunderstood these instructions, but personal feedback and advice by the moderator was given to that centre.


Part B is the first conversation.  Its contents should cover the topic of Part A.  The teacher thus needs to be prepared to
ask the candidate questions and give enough time for the candidate to answer.  It is very important that in Part B as well
as  in  Part  C  the  candidate  needs  to  ask  the  teacher  at  least  two  questions.    Should  the  candidate  not  do  this  close  to
the end of each conversation, the teacher must prompt the candidate to do so.  Questions asked by the teacher should
be on AS level, specifically asking for reasons and explanations.  Occasionally, teachers asked ordinary level questions.
This part of the speaking examination should be spontaneous and not learned off by heart before the time and it should
not be longer than seven minutes.

Part  C  is  the  second  conversation  which  also  should  last  about                          seven  minutes.   Altogether  the  speaking  examination
should   thus   be   close   to   17   minutes   long,   but   definitely   not   longer   than   20   minutes.     The   candidate   needs   to   ask   the
teacher at least two questions in this section as well.  Should the candidate not do this close to the end of this part of the
conversation, the teacher must prompt the candidate to do so.  If only one question is asked during each conversation,
the maximum mark for this category is 3 marks out of a possible five.  When no questions were asked, no marks could
be   obtained.      In   both   conversations   the   questions   that   are   put   towards   the   teacher,   should   have   to   do   with   the   topic
being discussed.  Some candidates asked their questions from Part B already in Part A, which is acceptable.  Teachers
should be aware that even though candidates have to ask them questions, teachers should keep their answers concise.
It     is     a     speaking     examination     for     the     candidates.          In     Part     C     questions     on     the     other     four     topics     for     that     specific     year
are   supposed    to   be   asked.      The   teacher   does   not   have   to   cover   all   four   topics.      Two   could    be   sufficient   as   well,   for
that   matter.      Neither   in   Part   B   nor   in   Part   C   the   answers   to   possible   questions   should   be   learned   off   by   heart.      Both
conversations should be spontaneous.

3.    GENERAL TEACHING SUGGESTIONS TO THE TEACHERS OF GERMAN AS A FOREIGN LANGUAGE
•     Once more it is of utmost importance to teach the candidates the different usages of “to have” and “to be” (haben
      und sein) in the perfect tense to let them achieve better marks.
•     The   modal   verbs   “to   be   allowed   to   –   can   –   must   –   should   –   to   want   to”   should   be   addressed   in   their   respective
      meanings and usages.
•     The double usage of writing something in the negative form is only part of the Afrikaans language, not part of the
      German usage.
•     You cannot use the “Umlaut” ä, ö, ü randomly for German words where a, o, u is required.  There is no such word
      as “Füßball” (Fußball, yes = football) or “Schüle” (Schule, yes = school) in German.
•     All Nouns and the beginnings of sentences                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               are always written with capital letters in German.
•     To avoid misconceptions, it is necessary to repeat the difference in meanings of the following words regularly in the
      lessons:  “dürfen und müssen (to be allowed to and to must), wenn und als (if and when), weil und von (because
      and from), für und vor (for and before), auf und aus (on and from  / out of / off), wir und uns (we and us)”.
•     Difference between the words “man” (someone) und “Mann” (man). Verbs for “man” (someone) are conjugated in
      the similar form as it applies to “er, sie, es” (he, she, it).
•     Rephrasing of texts can be exercised with indirect speech:  Der Autorsagt, dass …

2.    COMMENTS ON INDIVIDUAL QUESTIONS

In the Writing Paper, all the topics are either discursive or argumentative.  During the year in which the German Foreign
Language    AS      level      is      taught,      the      teachers      are      presented      with      five      topics,      as      can      be      seen      below.            For      the      essays
however,    under    each    topic    a    specific    aspect    needs    to    be    written    about.       This    is    the    title    of    each    essay    that    is    to    be
written.  Candidates should write the title on top of the page, not the general topic.  Therefore, it can be said, that some
candidates  wrote  about  the  topic  instead  the  specific  title,  or  only  ever  so  slightly  touched  on  the  title.    If  a  candidate
only wrote about the topic, but disregarded the exact title, then no marks could be awarded for the content.  This also
affected the language mark, however, in most cases some marks could still be awarded for language.  With regard to the
marking grid, the language usage should reflect authentic German. If the essay contains other European grammatical
structures or vocabulary, it definitely influences both the Content and the Language mark.

Writing an essay consisting of 250 – 400 words needs to be practised extensively.  Candidates writing this examination
might   not   have   reached   the   correct   number   of   words   as   only   one   page   with   lines   was   provided.      Others   “solved”   the
problem     of     not     having     enough     writing     space,     by     either     requesting     a     second     exam     booklet     or     some     candidates     just
continued   with   writing   their   essay   on   the   blank   page   at   the   back   of   the   examination   paper.      Blank   pages   are   actually
supposed to be used for planning.  However, enough writing space will be provided in 2024 examination.  Candidates
who did their planning, delivered an essay of better quality, thus also planning should be practised more extensively.  It
is essential that candidates do divide individual thoughts into paragraphs for their final examination, as the mark scheme
awards    marks    for    a    clear    structure:        introduction,    paragraphs    for    every    new    aspect    of    thought    and    a    conclusion.        In
the  introduction  candidates  should  mention  the  title  to  adjust  their  thinking  process  to  the  title.   The  conclusion  should
contain a clear point of view.

German    Foreign    Language  AS    candidates    may    give    their    opinion    in    the    introduction,    but    still    need    to    write    a    proper
conclusion.

      Reisen und Tourismus

Topic 1 was the most popular.

Topic 2 was the second most popular.

Topic    3    and    4    were    the    least    popular,    as    only    a    few    candidates    chose    to    write    on    these    topics.        For    both    topics    the
quality  of  the  essays  was  satisfactory,  as  in  both  cases  not  the  whole  title  was  covered  by  the  candidates.   All  essays
emphasized one part of the topic.  Candidates should be reminded to bring arguments for both parts of each topic.

With    regard    to   Topic    5    it    could    be    mentioned    that    none    of    the    candidates    who    chose    this    topic    understood    the    term
“Erzabbou” and only focused on the conservation of nature.

Some vocabulary and grammar aspects to which the teachers should pay more attention to:
•     Sport treiben (nicht:  Sport machen)
•     the difference between mögen and machen
•     günstiger (nicht:  mehr günstig; Steigerung needs to be practised more)
•     Fitnessstudio (nicht:  Fitnessstudium;  Studium is something else)
•     the difference between lieben and leben
•     the difference between Lehrer, Lernende, lehren und lernen, unterrichten
•     the difference between gebrauchen and verbrauchen
•     the difference between wenn and als
•     the difference between Umwelt and Umfeld and Umgebung
•     Sport (nicht Sports)
•     schlecht (nicht slect or any other wrong spelling)
•     Computer is still written with a capital C in German as it is a noun
•     the clear distinction between wir and uns
•     Ökonomie (not Ekonomy), a good synonym would also be Wirtschaft
•     arbeiten (not werken)
•     The following grammar needs attention:
      -      zum Beispiel (Beispiel with a capital letter, as it is actually zu dem Beispiel, thus a noun)
      -      the verbs for “man” (somebody / anybody) conjugates the same way as er, sie, es and takes on the neutral
             “sein” pronoun
      -      the use of definite or indefinite articles: most schools = die meisten Schulen
•     Sentence structure needs to be practised more:
      -      …., weil ……. Verb or then the Modal- or Hilfsverb at the                                                                           end
      -      …, dass …….. Verb or then the Modal- or Hilfsverb at the                                                                           end
      -      how to construct a proper German sentence in general
•     avoid the double “no” from Afrikaans; in a German sentence there is only one “nicht”
•     Candidates     “helped     themselves”     by     translating     some     expressions     directly     into     German.          By     using     these     direct
      translations,    they    do    not    write    authentic    German,    e.g.,    In    Konklusion    (Zum    Schluss),    Skills    (Fähigkeiten),    Futur
      (Zukunft), in meine Meinung (meiner Meinung nach)

Some issues raised here should be taught extensively in the lower grades already.

     How	predicting	floods	is	possible
     Meteorological	Predictions:	 One way to predict floods is through meteorological forecasts.  By analyzing
     weather patterns and conditions, meteorologists can identify areas at risk of heavy rainfall that may lead to
     flooding.  This advanced warning enables authorities to take preventive measures in flood-prone regions,
     such as reinforcing riverbanks or implementing evacuation plans.

     River	Monitoring	Systems:	  Installing  river  monitoring  systems  can  provide  real-time  data  on  water  levels,
     flow    rates    and    other    relevant    parameters.        By    continuously    monitoring    rivers,    authorities    can    identify    rising
     water  levels  and  take  prompt  action  to  prevent  flooding.   This  may  include  opening  spillways,  adjusting  dam
     releases or diverting water to reservoirs, to prevent rivers from overflowing.
     Floodplain	Mapping:	 Accurate floodplain mapping is crucial for predicting and preventing floods.  By
     mapping areas prone to flooding, communities can implement land use regulations, construction codes and
     zoning laws to prevent development in high-risk areas.  This proactive approach helps protect both lives and
     properties by avoiding potential flood damage.

     How	preventing	rivers	from	flooding	works
     Dams	and	reservoirs:	 Construction of dams and reservoirs helps regulate the flow of water in rivers and
     prevent flooding.  They store excess water during periods of heavy rainfall and release it in a controlled
     manner, reducing the risk of flooding downstream.

Flood	control	channels:  Building flood control channels or canals diverts excess water away from populated
areas and directs it towards less vulnerable locations or bodies of water.  These channels are designed to
handle large volumes of water and prevent it from inundating surrounding areas.
Levees	and	floodwalls:  Constructing levees and floodwalls along riverbanks and coastlines acts as
a physical barrier to prevent water from overflowing and flooding nearby areas.  These structures are
specifically designed to withstand the forces of floodwater and protect communities.

Sustainable	drainage	systems:		Implementing sustainable drainage systems, such as permeable
pavements, rain gardens and green roofs helps manage stormwater runoff.  These systems allow rainwater
to be absorbed into the ground or stored
Disagrees	that	it	is	possible	to	predict	floods	or	prevent	rivers	from	flooding/agree	to	a	low	extent.

How	predicting	floods	is	not	possible
Complex	Weather	Patterns:  Predicting floods requires understanding and monitoring intricate weather
patterns, including precipitation, wind direction and atmospheric pressure.  These patterns can be highly
variable and challenging to predict accurately, making flood forecasting difficult.

Limited	Data:	 Flood prediction relies heavily on historical data, such as river levels and rainfall records.
However, in many regions, such data may be scarce or incomplete, making it challenging to build accurate
models for flood forecasting.
Human	Factors:	 Human activities, such as land-use changes, urbanization and deforestation greatly
influence flood patterns.  These factors are often difficult to incorporate into flood prediction models, as they
require detailed knowledge of local conditions and behaviour.

Uncertain	Climate	Change	Effects:		Climate change introduces additional uncertainties into flood prediction.
Rising temperatures can lead to increased rainfall intensity and changes in weather patterns, making it difficult
to forecast future flood events accurately.
How	preventing	rivers	from	flooding	does	not	work

Inadequate	or	poorly	designed	flood	control	structures:	 If flood control measures such as dams or levees
are    not    properly    designed    or    maintained,    they    may    fail    to    control    the    flow    of    water    effectively    during    heavy
rainfall.  This can result in flooding even with these structures in place.
Insufficient	maintenance:	 Regular maintenance of rivers, including dredging and debris removal, is
essential to prevent blockages and ensure proper water flow.  If maintenance efforts are inadequate or
neglected, the risk of flooding increases.

Limited	capacity	of	flood	control	infrastructure:  Flood control infrastructure, such as reservoirs or
flood channels, may have limited capacity to hold excess water during heavy rainfall.  If the infrastructure is
already at its maximum capacity, it may not be able to control flooding adequately.
Lack	of	comprehensive	planning:	 Effective flood prevention requires comprehensive planning and
coordination among different stakeholders, including government agencies, local communities and experts.
If there is a lack of coordination or a failure to implement comprehensive flood prevention strategies, the
methods do not prevent rivers from flooding

Agricultural	conservation:	contour	ploughing.

Advantages
Soil erosion control:        Contour    ploughing    helps    to    prevent    soil    erosion    by    slowing    down    the    flow    of    water
across the field.  By ploughing along the contours, the furrows act as mini-dams, trapping water and preventing
it from gaining speed and carrying away valuable topsoil.  This helps to maintain the fertility of the land and
prevent soil degradation.

Water	conservation:	 Contour ploughing also aids in water conservation.  By following the natural contours of
the land, it allows for rainwater to be evenly distributed across the field, reducing runoff and increasing water
infiltration.  This ensures that the soil retains more moisture, making it more resilient to drought and reducing
the need for irrigation.
Disadvantages

Limited	effectiveness	on	steep	slopes:	 Contour ploughing is not as effective on steep slopes as it is on
gentle slopes. The plough may not be able to follow the contour line accurately, which can lead to erosion and
loss of soil on the steeper sections.
Increased	labour	and	time	requirements:	 Contour ploughing requires more time and effort compared to
traditional ploughing methods.  Farmers need to plan carefully and mark contour lines before ploughing and
may need to make repeated passes to achieve the desired contour effect.  This increases the labour and time
required for ploughing.

AOA:     Knowledge covers the biggest portion and for teachers to improve the learners’ knowledge on the content
regular assessments must be given, preferably after each topic.  Teachers must emphasize key words within definitions,
descriptions and explanations.

understanding of the content.

answers and reason.  The skill of making evaluations should be practised within assessment tasks throughout the year.

1    GENERAL COMMENTS
     In general, the examination paper was deemed fair.  Most candidates answered questions related to the
     Paris Peace Conference, the collapse of international order in the 1930s, and the Cold War.  Nevertheless,
     candidates should refrain from limiting themselves to specific topics and explore all the questions provided.
     A few candidates attempted to answer questions 4 and 6, which they were ill-prepared for. Questions
     1, 2, 3, and 5 elicited better responses from most candidates.  The markers observed a considerable
     improvement in how candidates answered part (b) and (c) questions compared to the previous years.
     However, some candidates still struggled with these questions.  Teachers must give equal attention to
     all the topics in the syllabus.  Most candidates avoided questions 4 and 6 because of the limited subject
     content knowledge.  Lastly, misinterpretation of questions was observed in question 2 part (a), where most
     candidates described how Hitler took over Austria instead of Czechoslovakia.  For question 3 part (a), most
     candidates confused the Atlantic Charter principles with the Yalta Conference.  As for question 3 part (c),
     most candidates confused the Berlin Wall with the Berlin Blockade.  In question 5, part (b), candidates'
     responses focused on why the Germans failed to establish a proper administration in Namibia until 1890
     instead of why the Germans came to Namibia.

Advice to take at heart:

1    Candidates should read the questions very carefully to ensure that their responses are relevant.

2    Dates given in a question should be noted so that only relevant material is included in the answers.

3    Candidates need to be aware of the specific demands of each type of question.

4    Part  (a) questions require recall and description.                                    Part (b) questions require recall and explanation, and
     part (c) questions require recall, explanation and analysis.
     In  part (c) questions the most effective answers argue both for and against the focus of the question and
     they also reach a valid judgement.  A valid judgement will go beyond restating what has already been written
     in the response by addressing ‘how far ’, ‘how important’, ‘how successful’ or ‘to what extent’, depending on
     the question set.

1    GENERAL COMMENTS
     Generally, the question paper was fair.  It is advisable to make sure that candidates obtain the skills to answer this
     paper.  Most candidates managed to score better marks in questions 1 and 5.  The comparison question is still
     problematic.  Candidates are still using the sources in isolation in answering this question.  The idea is for candidates
     to look at the similarities and differences between the sources.  The similarities and differences identified must be
     supported with evidence from both sources.  Candidates must provide valid contextual knowledge to explain why
     there are differences and similarities.  Candidates need to work on their purposes.  Most candidates still struggle
     with the evaluation questions.  Teachers/Tutors must address the following:  choices must be made where needed,
     e.g., support and not support/agree and disagree, etc.  Candidates must not use words in the sources to make valid
     inferences or assertions but rather infer from the sources.  Inferences, assertions and purposes made should be
     accompanied by support from the sources.  Contextual knowledge must receive a lot of attention.  Many candidates
     showed a lack of contextual knowledge which caused them not to score high marks because they could not
     properly interpret the sources.  Assessing a source's reliability is another aspect which requires a lot of attention.
     Candidates cannot afford to accept everything a source tells them as completely reliable and true.  When testing
     the source for reliability, the following four elements must be addressed: the author, the date, the audience and the
     purpose.  Question 5 carries a high number of marks.  When answering it, candidates need to directly check each
     source against the hypothesis given in the question and not against something that is similar to it.  They must make
     a choice and provide the support by copying directly from the sources and use their contextual knowledge to give
     an explanation.  When analysing visual sources such as cartoons, posters and photographs, candidates  should
     try to interpret sources by looking carefully at who wrote it, when, why and for what purpose.  There are two bonus
     marks available in the last question for assessing or reassessing the RELIABILITY of some of the sources they are
     considering.

     Reliability is a source evaluation skill which asks you to draw a conclusion about the trustworthiness of a source.
     Here is an example on how an evaluation/testing of the reliability of a source should be done:

Source A
The source is reliable:

Explanation:  As the author was present at the event, his record of it is likely to be very trustworthy.

NB; the Candidate must indicate on paper whether the source is reliable or less reliable. It is advisable to
present a balanced answer.
Author:  The author is unknown (why) to inform people about the events that happened at Sharpeville in 1960.

Date:  It was published in 2000, (why) after South Africa has become a democracy and it was safe to publish the
textbook.  Democracy came along with freedom of speech and freedom of the press which made it easier for the author
to express his/her views on the Sharpeville Massacre.
Audience:  the world/South African people (why) to educate them on the impact of the Sharpeville killings of 1960 and
to learn from it, not to repeat such horrible incidents in the future.

OR
The source is less reliable:  It could have been changed over the years to suit the author ’s view.

Author:  The author is unknown (why) to inform people about the events that happened at Sharpeville in 1960.
Date:  It was published in 2000, (why) because many people could have passed on by then and would not be able to
air their view about the events or to question the author ’s view.
Audience:  the world/South Africans (why) to educate them on the impact of the Sharpeville killings of 1960 and to carry
it over to the next generation in the author ’s view which might not represent what happened at Sharpeville in 1960 or to
justify retaliation or the apartheid system.

Example of Cross Reference:
Cross-referencing entails making direct connections between two or more sources by identifying and
examining areas of agreement and disagreement between them, with reference to specific examples from the
sources.

Linking statement:  Source A and C confirm the killing of blacks at Sharpeville police station.
Linking statement:  Source D and A both show that the people at Sharpeville peacefully protested.

fire.”

      knowledge.  Learners should show their understanding of the main message of the source, and

      can be answered better if one looks at the shortcomings (limitations) in the sources.

11    To answer the last question, follow the same principle as ordinary level by making a choice
      and copying the sentence or phrase that fits with your choice but you need to explain why the
      support for your choice is supporting or rejecting the statement/hypothesis.  To give a proper

Question 2
The responses to the question were generally satisfactory, with most candidates accurately identifying the
source's intention to condemn and expose the cruel actions of the Nationalist Government.  This was in order
to gain worldwide sympathy and end apartheid rule.  However, a few candidates struggled to support their
purpose with evidence from the source and instead arrived at a purpose not directly related to the year 1960.
Only a small number of candidates were able to attain Level 4, which required precise and comprehensive
evidence from the source to justify their purpose.
While a few candidates were able to achieve Level 5, which required valid contextual knowledge in their
interpretation of the source, the majority lacked contextual knowledge, as evidenced in their answers.  It is
important to note that sources cannot be properly interpreted without using one's knowledge of the context
in which they were created.

Question 3
Most of the candidates demonstrated an understanding of the usefulness and less usefulness of the sources.
However, some lacked contextual knowledge, cross-referencing skills, and the ability to evaluate sources.  It
is important for teachers to guide their learners in making better choices and utilising appropriate support
to make valid assertions.  Candidates must be able to identify the strengths and clarity of sources, as well
as understand that the limitations of sources can make them less useful.  After analysing both sides of each
source, candidates should be able to provide a conclusion on which source is more useful.  Cross-referencing
is an essential skill that should be emphasized.  It was expected of candidates to test sources for reliability, but
several did not in order to score more marks.

Question 4
A      significant      number       of      candidates      faced       difficulty      in      answering      the      question      effectively       as       they       failed      to
recognize the decision presented in Source E.  This resulted in a challenge for them to compare the sources,
and many ended up treating them in isolation.  While a few candidates were able to identify and address one
side, such as support or not support, with valid assertions and evidence from the sources, others merely
copied the correct support without providing any assertions.  Moreover, a considerable number of candidates
lacked contextual knowledge and used information from other sources, which is not permissible.  It is vital to
provide valid inferences for both similarities and differences between the sources, with supporting evidence
from both sources.  This emphasizes the importance of contextual knowledge in thoroughly analyzing and
interpreting sources.

Question 5:
The question was well answered by many candidates who demonstrated a clear understanding of how certain
sources either supported or opposed the hypothesis that only black Africans opposed apartheid during the
1960s.  The best answers shared common characteristics, such as identifying each source and its stance on
the hypothesis, focusing on the hypothesis itself, analyzing each source individually, and utilizing source
details to support or refute the hypothesis.

Most candidates were able to reach level 3 by addressing both sides of the hypothesis, while some only reached
level 2.  A handful of candidates included unnecessary contextual knowledge and cross-references in their
answers. Only a select few candidates correctly evaluated the reliability of the sources used.
At the NSSCAS level, it's important for learners to offer a well-crafted explanation that effectively connects their response
to the provided source. The explanation should showcase their contextual knowledge and relevance to the question at
hand.

It's worth noting that the pictorial source should only contain three key elements: the choice, a valid inference, and
support from the visible content or caption (if clear).  In instances like this, a separate explanation may not be necessary
as the valid inference can function as an explanatory tool.

The paper was of similar standard as that of last year. The marks ranged from 0 to 75.
It was noted that there was a general improvement in the presentation of work compared to the previous years.
Candidates are putting effort in showing working instead of writing answers only as was often seen in the previous
years. Teachers are commented for this positive development and should continue to urge the learners to show working.

Areas that still need improvement.
1.   Candidates are encouraged to cancel any abandoned work before attempting to answer the question again. If two
     answers are left on the same question, then the first answer seen will be marked.
2.   For candidates who use the additional page for answering a question, they must also cross out clearly the abandoned
     work and direct the marker to the additional page. The question number should be clearly written on the additional
     page before the learner answers the question. Again if the original work from the previous page is not cancelled,
     then the answer on the additional page is treated as a choice and the rule of first answer seen will apply.
3.   For questions that require candidates to show or prove a quoted answer, candidates are encouraged to show all the
     necessary steps and state the quoted answer at the end.
4.   Learners should not try to write answers in different forms unless the question requires them to do so. Once they
     have arrived at an acceptable answer they must stop there and avoid spoiling correct answers by attempting to
     rewrite answers in an alternative form.
5.   It was noted with concern that a number of candidates are failing to copy the figures correctly from the questions.
     Learners who misread numbers do not score maximum marks even if their method is correct.
6.   Learners are discouraged from using pencils when answering. They must strictly use a blue or black pen as
     indicated in the instructions to candidates.

General Comments:
The paper was of a similar standard to that of last year.  The marks ranged between 0 and 75.  Most candidates finished
the  paper.  It  was  clearly  noticed  that  a  significant  number  of  the  candidates  who  entered  this  syllabus  without  a  solid
algebra foundation, struggled to cope with the majority of topics.  Many candidates struggled with basic Ordinary Level
competencies, like the factorisation of trinomials and basic logarithmic laws.
It    should    be    noted    that    the    emphasis    in  AS    is    more    on    the    method    and    the    mathematical    process    than    on    the    final
solution. Complete methods should be shown at all times.
Candidates must make sure to delete work that they do not want to be marked at the specific question. It was often seen
that a candidate approached a problem in two or three different ways, without deleting any of the work. It was also often
seen that questions were replaced on the additional pages, without deleting the work at the original question. In these
cases, the work at the original question was marked.
If      candidates      want      to      use      the      additional      pages,      they      should      clearly      refer      to      the      additional      page      at      the      appropriate
question.
Candidates should be discouraged to work in pencil first and then to rewrite their work in pen. They often do not copy
the pencil properly and some accuracy is lost after the pencil is erased. In addition, it is more work and can result into
candidates not finishing the paper.
Centres   must   NOT   provide   any                                                            additional paper.   Candidates   do   their   work   on   these   papers   and   then   just   copy   the
answers, which results in the loss of all the marks for the specific question.
It  is  advised  that  answers  should  be  left  exact  where  possible. An  answer  of  ln  3  is  exact  and  is  preferred  above  the
decimal version of 1.098612… . Candidates should be encouraged only to round their                          final answer. This prevents the
loss of accuracy caused by premature rounding.
It was noted that some candidates used calculators that can                                                                                                                                                                                                               solve cubic equations. Candidates who use these, must
be taught to show all the steps of their working. No marks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 are awarded if only answers are given.
Most candidates took care to show their working, which allows them to gain marks for correct methods even when their
answers are wrong. However, candidates should be encouraged to show complete methods, especially when they are
asked to prove a quoted answer. Candidates may NOT work backwards from the quoted answer.
Candidates should realise that questions are structured in an attempt to help them. The earlier parts of a question are
often used in subsequent parts. The word “HENCE” is an indication that the previous answer must be used in order to
solve the specific question. Candidates must be taught how to interpret questions of this nature. If the question states
“hence” and the previous question is not used, no marks may be awarded for the solution. It should be noted that none
of the questions in this paper read “…hence, or otherwise, ….” If the “…. or otherwise….” is seen it is an indication that
the  previous  answer  should  assist  the  candidate  to  solve  this  question  easier,  but  there  are  other  (more  complicated)
methods that could be used.
More care should be taken in the classroom with the mathematical notation and the teaching of the relevant terminology.
Teachers  and  learners  should  not  only  concentrate  on  the  final  answer,  but  also  on  the  accuracy  of  the  mathematical
writing. For example, it was often extremely difficult to decide whether a candidate meant sin2x or sin 2x.
Teachers     should     please   not create their own abbreviations,     similar     to     those     used     in     social     media     language,     that
candidates are allowed to use in class. They should be taught that they may not use these abbreviations in any formal
mathematics assessments.
Teachers should take more care in the teaching of degrees and radians in class. It is not advisable to teach candidates to
work only in degrees and then to convert the answers to radians. Candidates must learn how to change their calculator
settings from degrees into radians. Candidates should be taught that they must immediately change their calculators to
the correct setting once they read a question.
Candidates should be taught with formula sheets in class. They should know which formulas will appear on the formula
sheet  and  which  formulas  they  need  to  study  by  heart.  It  was  very  often  seen  that  formulas,  derivatives  and  integrals
appearing on the formula sheet were quoted wrongly.
Candidates should take care NOT TO CHANGE the given variable, i.e.,                                                                                                                                                                                                             θ on the question paper cannot be changed to
x or A. If the formula sheet is used, the variables used on the formula sheet must be replaced for the relevant unknown
of the specific question.
Many candidates were very careless with the rounding instructions throughout this paper. It is always advisable to write
the complete answer, before the attempt to round.

1    Key messages
     •	    Candidates	should	be	encouraged	to	read	the	command	words	used	in	each	question	carefully.		For	example,
           “state	and	explain”	indicates	that	an	explanation	is	required	as	part	of	the	answer.		In	this	case	it	is	essential
           that	candidates	avoid	giving	only	a	statement	without	any	supporting	explanation.

     •	    Candidates	should	be	encouraged	to	learn	precisely	certain	definitions,	laws	and	principles.		The	omission	of
           a	single	key	word	can	lead	to	marks	not	being	awarded	if	it	is	an	important	part	of	a	definition.
     •	    Candidates	should	avoid	prematurely	rounding	interim	answers	within	a	calculation	as	this	can	lead	to	the	final
           answer	given	on	the	answer	line	being	incorrect.

     •	    Please	note:		Numerical	answers	may	not	be	given	as	fractions,	in	terms	of	pi	or	in	surd	form.		Although	this	is
           more	accurate,	candidates	must	show	correct	rounding.
     •	    Candidates	should	use	the	number	of	significant	figures	in	the	question	data	as	a	guide	to	the	                             number	    of
           significant	figures	required	in	the	final	answer.	In	the	vast	majority	of	cases	a	minimum	of	two	significant	figures
           is	appropriate	for	the	final	answer.
           Please	refer	to	the	syllabus,	page	5,	bullet	5	of	Arithmetics:		“take	account	of	accuracy	in	numerical	work
           and	handle	calculations	so	that	significant	figures	are	neither	lost	unnecessarily	nor	carried	beyond	what	is
           justified.”

     •	    Candidates	should	pay	particular	attention	to	the	prefixes	of	units.		It	these	are	ignored	or	interpreted	incorrectly,
           it	can	lead	to	a	power-of-ten	error	in	the	final	answer.
     •	    It	is	important	that	candidates	present	the	steps	in	their	calculations	in	a	clear	and	logical	way.		They	should
           explicitly	state	the	subject	of	any	equation.		If	an	equation	is	rearranged,	the	new	subject	should	also	be	stated.
           This	will	allow	any	correct	working	to	be	credited	even	when	the	final	answer	is	incorrect.

     •	    Many	questions	at	AS	Level	require	candidates	to	perform	unit	conversions,	for	example	from	mm2	to	m2	or
           from	g	to	kg.		Errors	due	to	incorrect	unit	conversions	can	add	up	over	a	number	of	different	question	parts	and
           make	a	significant	difference	to	the	final	mark	for	the	paper.		Candidates	should	continually	practise	converting
           between	units	when	performing	calculations.

     •	    In	‘show	that’	questions,	all	the	steps	in	the	solution	must	be	shown.		Full	credit	cannot	be	awarded	if	key	steps,
           such	as	the	rearrangement	of	an	equation,	are	not	shown.

     •	    Candidates	should	be	encouraged	to	write	their	responses	only	                     in	the	answer	spaces	provided.	 	          If	part	of
           a	response	is	unavoidably	written	elsewhere	in	the	answer	booklet,	it	should	be	clearly	labelled	so	that	the
           Examiner	knows	which	question	it	belongs	to.
     •	    Many	candidates	answered	in	pencil	first	and	had	to	rewrite	everything.		This	is	very	wasteful	of	valuable	time.
           Many	candidates	did	not	have	enough	time	to	rewrite	answers	and	were	not	awarded	any	marks	for	answers
           written	in	pencil.		Many	candidates	also	did	not	have	enough	time	to	erase	the	pencil	answers,	which	made	it
           very	difficult	to	read	and	could	result	in	marks	being	lost.

     •	    Candidates	should	be	advised	to	never	round	given	numerical	values.
     •	    It	is	important	that	candidates	practise	answering	questions	that	are	of	the	same	standard	as	those	in	the
           examination.		Working	through	past	papers	is	a	way	of	achieving	this.
